titleStmt.title: Interview with Atwood Rawlin Timmons, Undated
titleStmt.author: Thomas J. Healy II

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Atwood Rawlin Timmons was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then if I say, okay, December 7th, 1941, do you remember that day? And then you'll say December 7th, 1941, I was whatever.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Okay. Yeah. All right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then I'll say, you know, what branch of the military were you in -- is that you or me? I bet that's me. I'm going to ___+ that little slide, I can hear that little ___, it's that film going off the ...

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: Am I in your way?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. I'm just going to try to get this --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: I can go there and wait, if you want me to.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No, that's fine. I'm just trying to get these phones taken care of. And hopefully I can get this.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: How did they choose all of these different people that you want to interview?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I have no clue.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: We have a commission, a veteran's commission.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And we ended up with -- we sent about 4- or 500 of these out, we got a couple 300 back. This was last year.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Umhum. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And -- hold on, one more time.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I had talked to Carney a couple years ago about this. He was up to raising money for the phone cards.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Who was?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Carney. The Lieutenant Governor.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He was -- he was raising what?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, we had a fund-raising for phone cards for just, for veterans and stuff, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You did, down here?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No. Up there. It was at Dover.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: ___+ and he would talk to me.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How long ago was that?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Been a couple years ago, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: We tried -- John came to me, John and I -- I've known John for years and years and years, and I did a history of the Wilmington Fire Department a couple of years ago which was a documentary that he was involved with. And when we went up and met -- at a governors conference he met with lieutenant governor of Rhode Island who was doing this oral history project. This was two years ago. And he came back and we got together, and he said, I would really like to do that here. And I said, fine, let's do it in a documentary. And so Tony sent everything out from the veteran's office up there and we got the questionnaires going. And probably just about a year ago, about August, September of last year, they started making the selections. Had enough of them in, they started making the selections. And then there was probably about 10 people probably on the committee from all -- from Kent, Sussex, and New Castle County and all over, and a couple of the ex-colonels and generals and those guys. So they're the ones that ended up with -- I think we ended up with 60 or 70 out of the bunch.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I was just wondering if they had picked in different areas of different importance.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. And I didn't want to get into that because I'm going to sort out my own areas, because there's a lot of guys that didn't even -- that didn't even answer these things, people that I grew up -- men that I was around through my dad. And a lot of the 198th, Coast Artillery guys that were from the University of Delaware and right here, there weren't a bunch of those that answered at all that I -- that I knew and that Mayor Bill McLaughlin in Wilmington, he didn't answer it. Turm Trivett (ph), who's a veteran, never answered it. So there's a lot of --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- other people that -- and I'm trying to spread it out where I have enough -- and it's basically not too much of your war efforts, it's basically a war effort -- a little story about your war efforts, but also what you want to let other generations know. I mean, this is part of your history right here. That's what we're trying to do is we're trying to tell a history story of the veterans in Delaware. And we're interested in where you grew up, how you grew up, how you went to war, when you came back what happened, how did you do -- all that kind of stuff. And just a little story, that's all it is. So we're going to do -- you'll hear from us again probably -- the 20th of October we're going to have something, if you can get up to Wilmington, we're going to have a -- just a -- it's just a presentation showing, it's going to be about 30 minutes, the lieutenant governor is going to be there, hopefully the governor will be there. It'll last maybe an hour or so. And we're going to have all of the vets that we have interviewed to date there. And then the final product will come out in May, for Memorial Day next year. So. And it'll come out a couple -- a couple different forms.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: VHS or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: We'll have VHS, we'll have CD -- I mean, we'll have the DVDs. We're looking at doing a book that basically has just the audio part that will come out on CDs. So eventually all the ones we did -- maybe everybody might not make it into the film documentary, but everybody will be in the records and the libraries. And if people want to listen to your interview, they can just plug your name in and listen to your interview, because that's what we're hoping to do. And then we're trying to get it spread out to some of the schools, because that's where we feel --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: That's right, yeah. I been in a couple of schools now, myself.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- because we feel that there's -- I'm just making these numbers out -- probably out of 10 kids right now today that are sophomores in high school, out of 10 there's probably three that are really interested about the war, or listening about it or whatever. And I think more and more kids need to listen about that stuff --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- and why you guys were the greatest generation, and maybe the greatest generation was one before you guys, through the Depression and all that stuff, so.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, wherever I've been, they've been very attentive, I tell you, listening and asking questions.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Are we ready? Here's what we're going to start out, we're going to start out with you're just going to give me your full name and then spell your last name.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Okay. My name, Atwood Timmons, Atwood R. Timmons, t-i, double m, o-n-s, my last name.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And I'm sorry I didn't tell you this before, you'll look at me or look in my direction.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I'm looking at you right --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He's better looking than I am --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah. I saw me up there a while ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: There you go. All right. Now, here's three questions that I'm going to ask, and you can just tell them in a little story. Okay?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The first question is, Where did you grow up? The second question is, Who are your parents and what did they do? And your third -- third question is, Do you have any brothers and sisters? And that's -- that's the first question. So.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: All right. Repeat that first question.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. It's where did you grow up. So you're going to say I grew up.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Oh. I grew up in the Millsboro area. I was born in Millsboro, and still resident of Millsboro. Location, anyway. And that was in 19 -- January 6, 1924, I was born in Millsboro.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, tell me -- okay, so now tell me, my parents were.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Oh. My parents was -- were named Fred V. Timmons, and he was -- 1937 he went to Millsboro to be the town officer. And he stayed in -- as the Chief of Police until 19 -- in his 1970s when he went to work on the sewer and the water commission, and then he finally retired I would say about '90 -- about 1990, somewhere in that area. And he was pretty well liked in Millsboro as being a police officer. He was fair and he had a lot of respect, and people really backed him up.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Sounds like he lived to a very ripe age.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: He died when he was 94. Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now your mom.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: My mother was Elizabeth

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Timmons, and she died in the '72, I think it was. And she was a good lady. And I think I patterned myself after her as far as being easygoing and -- and not too rambunctious.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- was your mom -- tell me about your mom and dad. They both from Delaware? Are they Delaware --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yes. My mother and father are both from Delaware. Father was born in Dagsboro area, and my mother was born in the Millsboro area. And she -- her maiden name was Hickman.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. How about brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I have no brothers and sisters at all. I'm the only one. I guess when I came along they thought that was enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Or as my grandmother said, you're spoiled rotten.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I wasn't spoiled rotten.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: As to what --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I was brought up in the era of 1924 to '29, and we appreciate what we had. And we lived a good life, you know, as far as had plenty of food. And all the extra niceties, you know, we didn't have, but we managed, which was okay. But did what we could.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- did you have a bunch of aunts and uncles?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yes, sir. Our uncles and aunts, my mother had one sister, two brothers, and of course offsprings all down the line, so. But I don't have any aunts and uncles and cousins left now.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. December -- well, okay. Tell me -- tell me then or let's go, before I ask you about that, tell me about where you went to school, the different schools you went to.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, I went to Millsboro High School at -- for the full 12 years and graduated, and that was as far as my education went. I never went to college, just the tutelage learning psychology while I worked at Hutchins (ph) Auto Supply for 42 years and 7 months, and that was an interesting job. Never a dull moment.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- what was I going to ask you. Tell me -- tell me what year -- what year did you graduate from high school?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: June of 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Now, December 7th, 19 -- let me repeat that. December 7th, 1941, do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: December the 7th of 1941, I do remember. I was -- when I heard about it I was in Dover with my friend Dilbert Carmene (ph), which did live right next door to me until he passed away, and I went to school with him up to the ninth grade. But we heard about it when we was in Dover.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember what you were doing in Dover?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Just riding around on a -- on a -- in the evening. And first play -- thing I noticed was the kid selling newspapers, and then -- then we picked it up from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Any reason you were in Dover?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Looking for girls.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That's okay. You can say that. How long have you two been married?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: 58 years.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. I think that's okay now, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: Always has been.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Looking for girls. Okay. That's a good one. I've been doing the same thing. How old were you, then?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I was born in '24, so that was -- I was born in '24, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you were a junior in high school?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That would have been December.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I was in 11th grade. Yeah, 11th grade.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right. What was -- and you were going to Millsboro High School then, right?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yes, I go to Millsboro High School.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me what -- what was, like, all your friend -- I mean, were you talking about it? Was it brought up in school? Did you -- could you wait to get into service? What was it like down in Millsboro during that date and time?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: In Millsboro the fellas were -- some of them was volunteering in different Navy and the Air Force and armies and whatever. Coast Guard. And myself, of course I was still in high school, and when I graduated, the first thing I did, I went to Glendale Morton and applied for a job and got it in June. And I worked there until October. And that's when I got my draft notice. Well, my opinion was if they needed me, they would ask for me, and I was hoping that I wasn't 4F. I mean, I wanted to go. But I figured that I'd let them have their way, and when they needed me they would call me and I would be ready to go. And that's the way I played it. But I did come home in October because I had my draft notice, and why I came home, I quit there because they wanted to change my draft board from Millsboro to Baltimore, and that was kept you working until the last day and then boom, you was gone, into the service. So I kind of goofed off a little bit and they kind of laid me off and I came home intending to go in the service in turn -- in two weeks. Well, they filled their quota and I didn't go back to work in Millsboro until March of '43, and then the new draft -- the draft came up again and I went to the Air Force. I was two out of 52 that went in the Air Force, and I stayed with them in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So carry me on from there how that went. Tell me, you know, when you -- when you -- when you left home you went up to wherever, then you went here and then you -- how you got into the Air Force and how you got into air crew and all that stuff. So just tell me that little story.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, I got into the Air Force by being drafted in the Air Force, continued and went to Fort Dix, and then from our basic training we went down to Florida, Miami Beach, Florida. And then I was set in the Air Force. I mean, it was kind of cut into the wind that I would be a mechanic. So then we started going to the schools. We went to Keesler Field, Mississippi, and took B-24 training. And that was, consist of 10 days of starting with tools and different parts of the airplanes and engines and electrical, hydraulics and all that, to be a late maintenance worker. In other words, to remove and replace if it became necessary in the field. And then we came back to Florida and had gunnery training, Panama City, Florida. And then we had come home on leave for a few days, went to Utah, and was assigned there to go to Tucson, Arizona, Davis-Monthan Field, to be gunnery training out on the desert, and we made bombing runs on the different dams around Hoover Dam and the different places of importance, we made dry runs on them and we fired the .50 calibers. And I was trained to spray ball, which hangs underneath the airplane, but only used it one time overseas in north Africa. They just set in there, just watch it just in case somebody to come up. But when I got to India then they took the things out and we flew with that spray ball. And -- and of course as far as the -- my jobs then, I ended up with no ball to stay into, so I was in the back with the side guns, and transferring all of the gas. Took me years to see how important I was, really. Just sort of idea that I had, if it hadn't been for me transferring gas, I may not have got home, so.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now did you -- what were you in? The B-24? Tell me --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: B-24s, yes. I was in B-24s the whole time. In fact, the total time in B-24 training and combat time was three -- 565 1/2 hours. Total.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, when you finish your training here, tell me about where your first, you know, where you left from, where you arrived over in Europe or wherever you were, how you got there, and how you got back -- I'm assuming that squadron, you guys all went over as a crew together.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So tell me a little bit about that and how that all started.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, let's see. We went together as a crew. We crewed up in Salt Lake City, that's where we had our full crew. Then -- and we went to, like I said before, down to Tucson and took our gunnery training. Then we left there and we hit Lincoln, Nebraska, and picked up a new B-24. And -- and the uniforms and things. And our plane was the only one out of several, I don't know how many it was, but several of them, that had summer clothing. The rest of them had winter clothing. So I began wondering, you know, what in the world's going to happen to us? They're going to send us to England, we're going to have this -- so much summer clothing, and then we're going to freeze to death. So anyway, we went to Lincoln, Nebraska. We hit Bangor, Maine, and then we went to Newfoundland. From Newfoundland we flew to the Asian islands, and the majority of the crew then deviated and went to England. We went south, we went to north Africa. We hit Marrakech, French Morocco, and we stayed there overnight at a little joint in town seeing how the other half of the world lived, which is kind of smelly. But then we hit Tripoli, stayed overnight there, and got to look around in Tripoli and how it had been bombed out. And, well, it was just a beautiful place that was sort of in shambles, you know. I always wanted to go back, but never did. Then we hit Cairo, and that was an overnighter. And someplace, it must have been in Persia, but after we left that we hit Karachi, and I got 10 days in the hospital from having some bad food, I think, along way, packed lunches along the way, some dysentery, so I was left there for 10 days, and I had to beat my way across to India. And I had tickets to Calcutta. And then from then on I had to go from there until it was at Dum Dum airport, I had to go to Dhaka with the best way I could find a way. So I hopped a mail plane and got over to Dhaka over to where the rest of my crew was and my clothing and everything. So I was left 250 miles short to bum my way up there. On up there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, you hadn't gone into battle yet at all?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No. I hadn't -- we hadn't gone into battle then.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: But now --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So tell me about how that all started and where your first battle was and what you felt going into that.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Let's see. My first experience with flying to combat time was when we was in Dhaka we were assigned to haul gas into China to the 14th Air Force. Now, why we did it with B-24s, because we were armed. The air transport command fellows had the C-47s, C-46s, and the different airplanes like that hauling gas where they had been armed. Well, the Japs were just picking them off all the time. In fact, if the Japs didn't get you, weather might, because that way we fly in that hump, and that was pretty treacherous. The weather was sometimes you couldn't see the sky nor the land. Other times it was -- you could see down plane, and it was, well, almost dead reckoning, you know, because, you know, the navigation as -- like it is nowadays. So we flew better than 105 hours doing that. Then the monsoons came along and we was grounded for a month or so.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, where were you flying? Where were you flying the first mission?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: We were flying out of Dhaka, India, into China. Now, we'd fly as far as ?Guilin,? China, and unloading about 3,000 gallons of gas, or just about enough to get back to Kunming, and refuel to come home, and come back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you carried those in your auxillary tanks?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Auxillary tanks, we had, let's see, the B-24 got four bomb bays. Three of the bomb bays had 390 gallon tanks of punch-proof fuel tanks in them, and the other bomb bay had, why, I don't know, had two P-40 tanks which held about 290 gallons apiece. So we was taking off with 3,000 gallons of high test gasoline. And we lost our pilot on one of those runs. I didn't happen to be on that when I was -- didn't need me that day on the plane so somebody else was filling the spots, and we lost our best -- good pilot. Good man.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Just the pilot?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Just the pilot. One fella jumped out, he was from another -- he was a First Engineer from another crew, his parachute strung out but it never inflated, you know, so he -- he got killed.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Where was that over?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: That was over the tea plantations getting -- before they left India, before they got out of India and into Burma into China.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you were flying from India -- that's interesting. This is real interesting, because I just never thought about the Japanese being up that far into China and all in that area. You sort of think that they're over a little bit further. So -- so where were they -- where were the Japs flying out of?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Now, on the Jap -- for the Japanese was coming from -- now, we hauled gas into ?Guilin?, and that -- our first initial stop to dump the -- most of the gas, and it was pumped out in 50-gallon drums and the 14th Air Force was sitting there with airplanes waiting for that gas to be put into them so they could meet the Japs as they was coming in. Now, they were in China then moving from -- moving west. This is about in central China. And of course we had to stay overnight, and sleep down alongside the runway with it -- in the regular barracks, like. And at dusk you could see, start seeing flashlights spotting all over, leading the Japanese planes in. Of course when they got there they didn't hit too much, but they were coming in anyway. And then what they -- the Japs was in Burma, wherever we flew over there was Japanese into. They was on the ground and in the air and what. But they never came too close to us because with 10 -- 10 -- well, four or five turrets on our -- at least 10 guns pointing out, .50 calibers, they was very careful how close they came, if they wanted to come up at all, so they wasn't bothering us.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, did you fly in groups or --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: We mostly flew separately. Because when you get in the weather over the mountains, over the Himalayas, then you were -- you couldn't see, so it wasn't no formation flying, you just had to make your way by yourself. You had no cover, no nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So where was the plane going -- so they lost the whole plane, apparently, right?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me about that a little bit.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, evidently --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It was your plane?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: It was our plane that went down in the tea plantations in India, and they -- one of the engines blew up. So then everybody bailed out, got out of there, the planes, but the pilot. Now, the pilot wasn't strapped in his seat, he was blown clear when it hit the ground. But he was, you know, dead on impact. They -- one of the fellows had bailed out, looked at the plane, was looking at the plane, and the plane started into a spin, or started, dipped, wing dipped, and it straightened up, and that -- then he was too close to the ground. He was -- that was it, he never even got out of the plane. He said the explosion blew him out.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So it was a -- it was -- he wasn't hit by -- there --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No, it wasn't hit. It was all -- the plane engine blew and then she -- she just had -- went down, that was it. And with 3,000 gallons of gas aboard, that was kind of a big explosion.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you were flying out of India?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How long did you stay in India, then, when you was flying those missions?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: We -- see, I arrived in India in May, middle of May, and we started flying right away. Put in about 10 missions into China until the monsoons came along and grounded most of us. So we -- you couldn't even take off. So that was -- that was the first segment of our flying. And then after that was over, then bombing into 20 Burma, all up and down Burma, and into Bangkok. That was Siam at the time, which is Thailand now, if I'm not too bad mistaken. And we -- I ended up flying 26 missions in the bombing Japs up and down railroads, road bridges, Mandalay where there was -- Japs was stranded on the island in the middle of the Mandalay and the only bridge had been knocked out. Well, on that particular mission we -- we went in about 10,000 feet, we was drawing flack, which wasn't too effective with us because we was just a little bit out of range. But while we were up there drawing the flack we had the P-38s was up there flying us cover, P-51s and some P-47s, and they was flying along with us at 10,000 feet when they seen this ack-ack coming from the ground. Then they took -- they dove in on them. And then -- well, you would be looking and you would see them disappear down, wouldn't they, blend right into the ground, and then a big explosion where they'd get the guns. So we were baiting the gunners, the Japs, too, that was for ack-ack, and they were taking them out of commission with their pursuit planes. Fighter planes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you -- how long did you stay on that base? So you were flying --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, now we stayed -- we stayed at Dhaka until we quit hauling the gas and went to bombing and went to Asansol, which is a little bit further west.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: In?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: In India. See, it was Bangladesh is where Dhaka was, and I don't know if it was still in Dhaka -- or Pakistan, or what it was. Asansol could have been now in Pakistan. It was all one big place, India, but now they renamed everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you had -- so that's where you stopped. Did you stay there the rest of the war, pretty much?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yeah. Until -- we stayed in Asansol until we got ready to come home, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So out of that base -- tell me about the base a little bit. Was it -- did you have -- were you in Quonset huts? Were you in tents?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No. On base, housing was six-man barracks for the enlisted men. And we had the -- we had six men, six enlisted men on as gunners and the engineers, and then we had four officers as a pilot and a copilot and the bombardier and the navigator, but we kept them separate. So we had -- we had six-man barracks. And thatched roof and everything, so. But we -- it was -- it was fairly comfortable. It wasn't nice as life. As far as one big drawback we had, the water, in the whole of India I was told at that time was only two wells that was drinkable straight from them wells. The rest of them was just off limits, you couldn't even wash your teeth unless you come out of lister bags. Lister bags was boiled water and put out in the heat and heat it up to 120 degrees, what everyday heat was during the summertime. And we were drinking hot water all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So nobody sent you air conditioners over?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No air conditioners. Now, some of the barracks, air conditions, they had the homemade, up in the peak they had -- one of the barracks was a large thatched hut. I don't know how many people even stayed in there, but it had a high peak into it. And they took a fan, hooked a fan up, and burlap with a drip water system onto it, and that the fan blew through there. So it was kind of a damp air-condition.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: But it did, you know, where we were at in Asansol was dryer weather, so. But in Dhaka it was just muggy all the time. It was in the jungle, really, Dhaka was.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So tell me about the, let's see, were you ever scared of losing your life or anything, or.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, as far as being scared, none of us was too frightened of not being able to come home, for at least myself, at least the first half. The first half of our time over there, well, say the first six months, we were just sort of happy-go-lucky, and, you know, go out with the plane, do our job. And we had flack vests, we wore steel helmets over, just like the infantry. And we never -- we never put the flack vests on. We always lay them on the floor and sit on them. But about halfway through we decided, well, now, we wouldn't mind coming home in one piece, so we started wearing flack vests. And we had, of course, our dress over any time. When we was in India we took off -- we went over to Bay of Bengal, and a lot of times 90 percent of the flight was over the bay, over water. So we had our normal clothes on, and, well, sometime we flew so low I just ?wore? short sleeves. But we had our normal clothes on, plus a Mae West, which was an inflatable life jacket, and then we had a flack vest. Underneath that we had a survival vest, and we had a belt that we kept around, had rupees into it and maps for getting out of the Burma or to get back, walk back home if you had to. Now, if you had anything happen to the airplane that you had to go down in the water, then on the east side -- on the west side of Burma, Bay of Bengal, there was the PBYs would be there to pick you up. On the -- on the east -- on the east side were Thailand or Siam, you know, and Vietnam and all those other were there on the other side, Isthmus of Panama -- not of Panama. Either it was the -- where they, end of Singapore, it was picked up by submarines. So but still on you -- but they had things you had in your jacket from different dialects of people you could take it and show to them and they could read the dialect in that area, and then they could escort you back home with -- and they paid off anything -- anybody rescued, it would be paid in cash. In American money, I guess, or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- how big was your squad -- tell me, what was -- what was the correct name of your, I guess, I don't know, was it a bomb group or -- your group. You were part of which Air Force and --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, I was in -- the Air Force that we was in, was under, was Tenth Air Force, Seventh Bomb Group. We was in the 492nd, I believe that's right, bomb squadron.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many -- was there -- how many planes in those squadrons? Is it the same as the rest of them, fifteen? Five?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Five, possibly. Fifteen, yes, fifteen in those -- in the squadron, yes. To tell you the truth, I'm not really sure. But we used to fly some tight formations, anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And these are the 24s?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So they got rid of the B-25s fairly early, right?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: B-25s was prevalent over there, too. Well, they had B-24s. At one time they had some B-17s over there, but the 24s were more of a workhorse than the 17s were. They were -- they could do, take more -- a bit more bomb loads and they would just, well, here lately, you know, lately there's an argument about B-17 over and B-24s or vice versa, whatever, but really they're just about the same. But they -- B-24 just a little bit more advanced than what the 17 was. But -- but as far as being a good workhorse, it was a good airplane for that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You were a gunner?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I was a gunner.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: But what was your primary duty?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: My primary duty in the 24 was transferring the gas.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Was coming under the assistant engineer. I stayed in the back, watched for torching engines and anything that was going bad there. And the gas had to be transferred from the outboard tanks into inboard, so it would be back -- it would be to keep the ship in balance so we could make it back to India, our main base. One time we had to land in India but it was probably right on the border, so we had to refuel there to get on back to the base at one time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, did you do your own check? Did you do your own -- when you had -- when you do the plane, what they call a check, when you bring it down and you go through your maintenance times? Did your crew do that or did you have --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, the First Engineer was in that. And of course in the ground crew, they would take over and do the inspections and everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What -- is there -- is there one or a couple of incidences that really stick out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Yes. When I applied for this I sent a thing, we got a citation for the longest flight in World War II up to that time, a bombing formation flight. Now, we left before daybreak, and we went -- well, the round trip consisted of 26 -- 700 miles. We was in the air 17 hours, between 17 hours 45 minutes to 18 hours. And we got that citation for that. And we never got over 1,000 feet flying to Bay of Bengal. We got to our target area, it was a bridge, about a three-spanner bridge, and we went in, flew one at a time around these -- this bridge on each end, and we come in about 500 feet, and then we'd do dive-bombing. The pilot had a crosshairs on his -- right in front of his face sort of like on his dash, and he put that crosshair on that target of that bridge, and he would drop a 500-pound bomb with a 10-second delay, and that give you a chance to get away from there before it blew up. And we just circle and circle and circle around that until we dumped all of our 500-pound bombs. Now, when we took off from India, we had, like I said before, four bomb bays. Three of them had 390-gallon tanks into them. The fourth bomb bay had six 500-pound bombs, and that's -- that was our bomb load that we carried down there. And that was a long mission. But sometimes they, if they flew too tight, it didn't happen on that mission but it has done on the past, in other missions, if we came along and dropped a 500-pound bomb at 300 feet, the next plane behind us was getting too close and his 10 seconds was up, when he got over the top of that bomb then he got bomb fragments. And we stopped in this one place to refuel one day and they -- we heard about this B-24 that had come in over a bomb that blew up underneath of them, shot the hydraulic system out. They landed the thing in this base, they got back to this base, but when they hit the ground the whole hydraulic, had one shot of the hydraulic, and when they took her off the side of the runway, that's where she stayed. She was junk. But nobody got hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How was your squadron? I mean, did your squadron pretty much all stay together? Was there anybody that was -- did anything go down during any of your missions or anything?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Now, we had -- more than missions or losses of airplanes, we had very few of them lost. Now, majority, anything that did happen that maybe we would leave and get a couple of hours out and something would be wrong with the engines, we'd go back, and over there and take our bombs -- well sometimes we would jettison our bombs so we could land without the things in there. But as far as losing too many, we didn't lose too many. Very few. And we was more susceptible in -- I would say half of my missions was at low level, 500 feet, 300 feet, and parachute wouldn't have been very good for you if you did have to bail out, because it takes a 20-foot chute usually at that time about 300 feet before it fully inflated to get you down safely. And so that was mainly what the main thinking was, it was the danger of it right there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, you got the -- did over 25 missions?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I did a total of 36. Ten of them was gas runs, but we were armed, and so they counted as missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So after, I guess after the 25th mission, you got your distinguished --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, no. No. On the -- the -- the medals was based on hourly. Now, the first 100 hours you got an Air Medal. Now, that, of course that consisted of hauling the gas and bombing, too, in Burma. And the -- so every 100 hours you got an Air Medal. 300 hours of time in the air you got DSC. So I had three hour medals and one DSC.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did it also give you a higher rank?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I did get to Staff Sergeant and that was for -- in order to get -- go up to Tech I would have had to become a First Engineer. But the rest of the time, we just -- it was automatic they come in to your time. But the thing of it, my 36 missions that I put in, 365 1/2 hours of it was bombing missions. So, you see, that was average 10 hours per mission, and of course that one, Bangkok was two times we been there was 14 hours, so.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- you're a pretty big guy, though, to sit in a turret.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I was only about 150 pounds, something like that. Still only about 155 pounds, undressed.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, it was one of those turrets that went down once you got in it it was two-bed? Did you lower down into it or did you crawl into it?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: In the spray ball, in the B-24 the spray ball, not like on the 17, the 17 is permanent down. On the 24, when you landed a 24, she's sitting on the -- on the runway, she's only about two foot off the ground, the bottom of her. So they was -- it was up inside the airplane, and you had to hand -- hand hydraulic it down to position, turn the guns down, straight down, then you had a little door there, double door, maybe 18 inches square, something like that, and then you crawled into that, and you sit in your seat, you reach behind your back neck, you snapped the thing -- you had a seat belt you fasten in there, and you were isolated. And you down in that thing in 24, when you would put your guns at level, then no one could see over the wing tips. So you down there, you was kind of isolated. You were down there by yourself. And in order to get out you had to turn your -- turn your guns straight down, undo your things from latch -- latches from the inside in your belt and you would crawl out, and then you would take and pump the thing back up inside. If it was left down, it would wipe it off on landing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Let's see. What -- what do you think the history books are leaving out about World War II?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: About World War II, they're leaving out, and I suppose from many other wars the same thing, just the history of it. Just the -- enough -- well, sometimes it's totally eliminated, and --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: {phone rings} Yes? Thank you. Okay.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: And then we've been going, I don't know if you knew Obrey (ph) Murray (ph) or not or heard his name mentioned.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Obrey (ph) Murray (ph), he was on this board, too, and he belonged to our post, the VFW post. And we had been together in Sussex Central, Georgetown, at one time last year and talking to one of the classes, very attentive, asking questions, and we -- he passed out some of his books for the right answers, you know, of course they were simple answers, they get to get a book. And I went a couple of years before that to Milford High School, and it was a packed classroom, 31 and the fellow up there had his father's collection of books of World War II and anything he could get his hands on World War II underneath the windows was lined with them. And he had us up -- five of us up there, and we gave a 10-minute spiel of -- of all we went through, you know, and started from time you went in to time you got out of service. And -- and all of them kids was -- well, she, my wife was there, and you hear no noise, you hear -- nobody went to sleep, and everybody was ears wide open. And some of the people over in Rehoboth VFW has been up in Pennsylvania where they were originally from and had talked to schools. They talked for an hour, there was three or -- three brothers of them total I think it was, and it took them another hour or more to answer the questions that them kids answered, and they was in the lower grades. And they answered all kinds of questions.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What -- what do you feel about putting -- having this in sort of a regular -- a regular course in high school?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: It should be done. Whether it be World War II, World War I, World War II, or Vietnam or up to the present time, it should be in there. The good things. All you're hearing now in some of this -- this Iraq thing is all things that -- bad stuff. You don't hear no good stuff, really. The good things that being done over there, they -- the news media just don't want to talk about it. Nothing but bad. I mean, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- oh. So tell me when you got home -- so tell me, okay, you stayed over in -- in India until you were released. Was that right after VJ day?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I came home -- I got -- we got to the states, I got done at Norfolk, Suffolk, Virginia, there by boat, took us 30 days to get home.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: 30 days?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: 30 days. It didn't take long flying over there, it took us 30 days to get home. So we landed there, and that was in July, and I came home. And while I was home, well, a little funny instant. Now, when you went into the service you walked out to the highway if you want -- or go into town by the base, wouldn't be many seconds, I mean seconds, before somebody was there, Where you going, Soldier? And they'd take you in town and drop you off, you know, or sometimes longer trips than that, you know, according to where you wanted to go. And so I could -- I could always get rides. And when I come home, I could get rides until I got to Milford. I had to call my father to come get me from Milford, from Millsboro to Milford to bring me home. So this VJ night I wanted to go to Georgetown. So I walked out to 113 and I stuck my thumb up for 20 minutes. Nobody would stop and pick me up to take me where I wanted to go, so -- where you want to go, you know. I turned around and come home and went to bed, and that's when Japs surrendered that night. So I missed all the stuff that, you know, celebrations by sleeping -- sleeping through it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, were you out at that time?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Huh-huh. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You weren't discharged?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I entered in August, and I didn't get out until October of the same -- of '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, did you go back -- from your leave, did you go back after VJ day to --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: My -- after I got done with my leave in August I went to Greensboro, North Carolina, and became -- well, while I was there they was -- the choice to either stay there, if it became a permanent, what they call a permanent party. You took a test, and I had taken the shorthand and typing in high school for two years, so I took the test and I passed -- I stayed in there. If I hadn't passed the thing I would have ended up in Texas. Well, I didn't want to go to Texas. It was too hot and sandy, but.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So when you finally got out, tell me how -- where you went back to work and you met your wife and all that stuff, and tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, okay. Now, when I -- when I got discharged from the service in October, latter part of October, just before Halloween of '45, I -- well, I went home -- I was at home, I got a phone call, and I had to worked at the mercan store in Millsboro when -- in the 11th grade, and when I came back, I missed the first draft so I had -- that's where I went to work again in there. And when I came home, Mr. Green, he's out of Milford and he was the mercan store manager, general manager of the whole area. He said, Atwood, he said, I want you to go to work in Milford as -- as assistant manager. I said, I just got home and I'd like to have a couple weeks off. If you want the job, you got it, give you ten minutes to call me back. I called him back in ten minutes, says, no, I want to be -- I want to be home on vacation for a while and do some running around for a couple weeks before I go to work. So then I went to work with Glendale Morton after that, and I worked with them for a year and a half, I guess it was. And I met her at a basketball game, and I liked what I saw, and rescued her from Milton, took her to Millsboro. And that's been going on now 59 years, coming this -- coming May of 2005.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And do you have any children?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Two. Two children. One boy, which is a mail carrier in Millsboro, and a daughter which is a nurse in Beebe Hospital. She went to work -- actually had two children, went to college up to Del Tech and become a nurse.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: And of course in the meantime I worked in Hutchins (ph) Auto Supply 42 years and 7 months.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- why do you think they call you guys the greatest generation?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Why do they call us the greatest generation? I -- could have been, I don't know, it was a turning point of the way things was being done in -- in the world as far as democracy was concerned, I suppose. I never gave it too much thought until I got reading, I can't even think of his name now, wrote three books, I got all three of his books.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Brokaw?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Brokaw, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Let's see. Did you sing a lot of songs, like, On the Road to Mandalay? You probably know that song.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, we had several songs that we sang while I was in basic training, but I forgot a lot of 'em {laughing}.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You heard that, "On the road to Mandalay where the flying fishes play"?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I don't know if we ever did sing that one or not, the Mandalay --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: "And the sun came up like thunder across the China Bay?" I would have been singing that on every mission.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: I don't think I -- I don't think I ever sang that one, no. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What do you want generations to come and know and remember about World War II?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Well, generations to come, like for them to know about what -- what was fought for as far as democracy was concerned, and maybe what they would learn about past histories of wars come in very handy for future conflicts, getting out of them without having to have a lot of bloodshed.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Now, the next one is a major message that you would leave for generations to come. Don't have to be about the war, doesn't have to be about anything, just your major message from you.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: A major message for the future to come, future to come. Well, a little thing at the VFW, I usually have been with the Voice of Democracy for several years, which we have a Sussex Tech at Georgetown as our school, and to hear some of the tapes that they make up there, and by doing research on this -- on the network, they picked it up that way, that's the only way they've got to doing it, they -- those pupils has, well, they're all over the United States, it's 52 states -- or 50 states and a couple of the -- more of the possessions, they are learning a lot of things about what to do as far as the, keeping the freedom like it is and what they would do in different situations. So I'd like to see more of that going on through the schools being taught than letting it just -- pushing it -- sweeping it underneath the rug. Not saying anything about it as if it never happened. Like the Holocaust, a lot of people don't even believe we had a Holocaust. Well, it was real.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Would you do it again?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Would I go back in the service again willingly? I would say I probably would, to fight for America and what it stands for. And protect -- and while I was doing it to protect the flag. That -- the flag is --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I guess god sent that down. Okay. That's good. That's good. Are you okay?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yep. Very good.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you want to do -- oh, no.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Photographed. Or copied. {Showing photograph.}

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: He even has a leather jacket --

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: -- with all of his insignias that he brought home.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: Original stuff on it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Timmons
sp.p: On the back you had the beaver.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: We called our squad Eager Beaver squadron. I didn't mention that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Hold on. I want to do -- I want to ask him one more question. Okay. Tell me -- that's what I was going to ask you. Did you have -- did you have any pictures on your plane or anything? Did you call your plane a certain person or Betty Grable or whatever?

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: No, we didn't paint none, no. We just had Eager Beaver squadron, but I don't think no painting onto it. We -- we model B being an older one, I think what they used to do, the better the pilot, the worse the airplane you got. We looked -- finished with that picture? You finished with that?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I'm going to put it right here, right where it was.

sp.speaker: Atwood Rawlin Timmons
sp.p: That far back? Some of that was put up by the church, too. That's why I put that in there. I even got letters back -- in fact, I even got money back in there, change I got when I was in China.
